chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar (may Allah be pleased with him) told us, saying: My father told us, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya ibn Imran al-Ash'ari, who said: Abu Abdillah al-Razi (and his name is Abdullah ibn Ahmad) told me, from Sajjada (and his name is Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abi Uthman, and the name of Abu Uthman is Habib), from Muhammad ibn Abi Hamza, from Muhammad ibn Wahb, from Abu Abdillah al-Sadiq, Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon them both), who said:

A wise man followed another wise man for seven hundred farsakhs in seven words, and when he reached him, he said to him: O you, what is higher than the sky, wider than the earth, richer than the ocean, harder than stone, of more intense heat than fire, of more intense coldness than severe frost, and heavier than immovable mountains? So he said to him: O you, indeed, the truth is higher than the sky; justice is wider than the earth; the soul's sufficiency is richer than the ocean; the heart of the disbeliever is harder than stone; the desirous, the greedy, is of more intense heat than fire; the despair from the mercy of Allah, Exalted and Glorious is He, is of more intense coldness than severe frost; and slander against the innocent is heavier than immovable mountains.
ai.seo_question: What are the seven things that are higher than the sky and heavier than mountains according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Mani al-Akhbar*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) elucidates the metaphysical weight of seven key spiritual states by contrasting them with physical extremes, a method reflecting the Shia tradition of using tangible analogies for abstract theological concepts. The text emphasizes that inner realities—such as the heaviness of slander on the innocent and the coldness of despair from God’s mercy—transcend the most formidable elements of creation, underscoring the primacy of the soul's condition over the material world.
